_note: SAMPLE recap content, generated from the hypothesised draft.

feature.headline: Nobody Left This Room Clean
feature.standfirst: Fifteen rounds, twelve managers, five quarterback hoarders, one tight end cult, and a kicker run that arrived about eight hundred players too early.

sections.heading: Mike Built A Quarterback Room, And Not Much Else
body: Mike opened with Jalen Hurts, then took Drake Maye, then Dak Prescott, then Jaxson Dart, then circled back in the sixth for Daniel Jones. Five quarterbacks. The format starts two. He didn't draft a team so much as install a depth chart and forget the rest of the building.

The knock-on effect is that his first running back showed up in the fifth round and his first tight end in the ninth, by which point everybody else had already picked over the useful ones. Every Sunday Mike gets to choose which three quarterbacks sit and watch. Somewhere in that house there's a lineup screen with more men under center than skill players, and he keeps refreshing it like the numbers might move.

sections.heading: Keshia Cornered A Market That Doesn't Exist
body: Josh Allen first overall is defensible. Matthew Stafford in the second is fine. Caleb Williams in the fourth, Jared Goff in the fifth, and Tyler Shough in the sixth is a man collecting stamps. Keshia took five quarterbacks before she took her second skill player, and one of them is a rookie who has to win the job first.

She and Mike between them took ten quarterbacks. Ten. In a twelve-team league where the position is scarce and everybody knows it, two managers decided scarcity was a thing to be owned rather than solved. The rest of the room simply waited for them to run out of roster spots, and eventually they did.

sections.heading: Bree's Badass Boys Are Mostly Tight Ends
body: Bree took Tyler Warren in the fourth, Colston Loveland in the fifth, Sam LaPorta in the seventh, and then Greg Dulcich in the thirteenth for reasons known only to Bree. Four tight ends for one tight end slot. That's not depth, that's a support group.

The other half of her draft is a running back committee assembled entirely out of guys who are one snap from being the guy: Rico Dowdle, Kyle Monangai, Aaron Jones Sr., Jacory Croskey-Merritt. And under all of it, one quarterback — Sam Darnold, taken in the sixth — holding up a superflex roster by himself. Three receivers, four tight ends, one arm. It's a beautiful, terrible building.

sections.heading: Colin Went Shopping In The Antiques Aisle
body: Travis Kelce in the seventh. Mark Andrews in the eighth. Isaiah Likely in the ninth. AJ Barner in the thirteenth. Colin looked at a position that pays for exactly one starter and decided to buy the whole wing of the museum, and two of the pieces are entering their thirties with a lot of mileage on the odometer.

Then there's the quarterback plan, which is Jordan Love and Malik Willis. One starter, and a backup whose main qualification is that he's played real snaps when everything went wrong. In a format that starts two quarterbacks, Colin's second one is an emergency measure he drafted on purpose.

sections.heading: Doug Drafted Every Running Back In America, Then Kept Going
body: Bijan Robinson, Jeremiyah Love, Kyren Williams, Bucky Irving, Bhayshul Tuten, J.K. Dobbins, Rachaad White. Seven running backs, five bench spots, and one flex slot to squeeze them through. Doug isn't building a roster, he's running a backfield with a waiting list, and half of it will spend the season inactive on his own bench.

The receivers came late and thin — Rashee Rice, then Stefon Diggs in the tenth, then a rookie in the thirteenth. Doug looked at a league where every other manager was fighting over pass catchers, decided none of that concerned him, and went back to the well. Again. The well is empty now. He checked.

sections.heading: Chenell Defends Her Belt With One Quarterback And Change
body: The reigning champ ran the most conventional draft in the room and it's still a mess in one specific way. Christian McCaffrey, Breece Hall, Nico Collins, A.J. Brown, George Kittle, DK Metcalf — a genuinely frightening starting lineup. Then the quarterback position, which she addressed in the ninth round with Geno Smith and in the twelfth with a rookie in Cam Ward.
So the plan is a title defense built on the best skill group anyone assembled and a superflex slot she filled the way you fill a form at the DMV. It'll probably work. That's the annoying part.

sections.heading: Jesse Paid A Fortune For Kicking And Nothing
body: The last two rounds of this draft were a stampede for defenses and kickers, and Jesse ran it hardest. He closed out with a defense and Brandon Aubrey after taking Josh Jacobs and Mike Evans in the tens — which is to say he spent his final two picks on units ranked in the nine hundreds while real bodies sat there.

He wasn't alone. Eleven managers took a defense in the fourteenth round, all within four picks of each other, like a fire drill nobody scheduled. Tyler, Colin, James, Justin, Mike and Evan then simply stopped, kickerless, walking out of the building without the one guy who's guaranteed to score. Jesse's three-quarterback opening — Brock Purdy, Kyler Murray, Baker Mayfield — at least gave him options. His running back room is Travis Etienne Jr., Jadarian Price, Jonathon Brooks and Tyjae Spears, which is less a room and more a hallway outside one.

teams.verdict: Three Quarterbacks, Zero Confidence In Any
teams.teaser: Jesse drafted Gibbs first overall and then spent the next three rounds assembling a quarterback committee nobody asked to serve on.
body: It starts clean. Jahmyr Gibbs at 1.01 is the pick anybody would make, and Jesse made it, so we'll allow him that one moment of peace. Then Travis Etienne, and then Brock Purdy, Kyler Murray and Baker Mayfield in three straight rounds, which is a strange thing to do unless you believe each of them is about to get benched by their real team. Jesse didn't draft a quarterback. He drafted an audition, and he's going to make three grown men compete for a job every Tuesday.

The running back room is where it gets personal. Jadarian Price, Jonathon Brooks, Josh Jacobs, Tyjae Spears — six backs total, stacked behind Gibbs like he's expecting the position to be outlawed. Brooks is coming off a torn ACL, and Jesse skipped healthy men to get to him. Somewhere in that pile is a flex spot that seats one. The receivers got the leftovers: Ladd McConkey in the seventh, Carnell Tate in the ninth, and Mike Evans in the eleventh, entering his age-32 season and still, somehow, the most reliable name on the list.

Then the finish. A defense at 14.12 and Brandon Aubrey in the last round, 790 spots past where anyone else on the board was sitting. That's the one honest pick of the day: Jesse waited until nothing was left, and took the guy who kicks. Fifteen picks, six running backs, three starting quarterbacks and one bye week he hasn't opened yet.

teams.verdict: Doug Drafted Every Running Back In America, Then Kept Going
teams.teaser: Nine running backs, one real quarterback, and a Sunday lineup that will leave five of them on the couch every week.
body: Bijan Robinson, Jeremiyah Love, Kyren Williams, Bucky Irving, Bhayshul Tuten, J.K. Dobbins, Rachaad White. That's seven backs before we mention that Dobbins has spent his career being carried off fields and White got taken with real players sitting there. Doug has built a bench with a team attached. Every Sunday he gets to pick which four of his running backs don't play, and the four who don't will probably outscore the ones who do.

The quarterback plan is Jayden Daniels and then, in the eighth round, Bryce Young. In a format that starts two. Doug looked at superflex, the single most quarterback-hungry setup in fantasy, and decided he'd rather own the entire Jacksonville and Tampa backfield depth chart. Bryce Young isn't a second starter. He's a coin flip with a helmet on.

The receivers are an afterthought and they know it. Rashee Rice in the fifth is fine. Then Stefon Diggs, Jalen Nailor and De'Zhaun Stribling, taken so late they're less a wide receiver corps than a rumor. Doug skipped twenty-nine better options to get to Nailor, which suggests he'd stopped reading names and started reading vibes. Cameron Dicker closes it out, 790 spots past reason, and by then the roster had already made its point.

teams.verdict: Keshia Cornered A Market That Doesn't Exist
teams.teaser: Six quarterbacks in a league that starts two, plus three tight ends for one slot, and a running back room of exactly two men.
body: Josh Allen, Matthew Stafford, Caleb Williams, Jared Goff, Tyler Shough. Then Allen again in your head, because you keep double-checking. Six quarterbacks if you're generous about Shough, and this is a league that starts two. Keshia isn't drafting a roster. She's hoarding a commodity in the hope of a shortage that a twelve-team league will never produce. Stafford's entering his age-37 season and he's the second-best asset in a pile that runs five deep.

The tight ends followed the same logic. Kyle Pitts, Dalton Kincaid, Brenton Strange — three of them, one lineup spot, and all three have spent their careers being described as about to break out. Keshia has assembled the entire genre of guy who's going to be good next year. It's not a position group. It's a support group.

Which leaves the running backs: Ashton Jeanty and Jordan Mason. Two. In fifteen rounds. Jeanty's a rookie and Mason got taken with nine better names still sitting there, so the plan appears to be that Jeanty never rests and never gets touched. The receivers are Courtland Sutton, Khalil Shakir and Makai Lemon, which is a fine bench for someone else's team. Harrison Mevis kicks. Somewhere a spreadsheet is open to a tab labeled RB and it's mostly white space.

teams.verdict: The Champ Built A Beautiful Team, Then Forgot Quarterbacks Exist
teams.teaser: Chenell drafted like the reigning champ for nine rounds and then remembered, faintly, that superflex starts two quarterbacks.
body: The front of this draft is genuinely mean. McCaffrey, Breece Hall, Nico Collins, Cam Skattebo, A.J. Brown, George Kittle. That's a real team. Collins went with twenty-two better names on the board and Chenell took him anyway, which is what defending a title does to a person — she stopped consulting the board and started consulting herself. DK Metcalf in the seventh with twenty-one better options is the same move, twice, and both times she looked like she meant it.

Then round nine happens. Geno Smith, entering his age-35 season, is the starting quarterback of the defending champion. Cam Ward, a rookie, is the backup. In a format that starts two, Chenell's Sunday plan is a 35-year-old and a guy who's never taken an NFL snap that counted, and she waited nine rounds to think about it. The best roster in the room has the worst position on the roster.

The rest fills in nicely enough. Jaylen Warren, Michael Pittman, Kenny Gainwell, Chig Okonkwo — depth that works, drafted by someone who clearly enjoys drafting. Jason Myers in the last round, where kickers belong, is the most professional thing anyone did all night. It's a title-winning roster with a quarterback situation held together by faith and a rookie.

teams.verdict: Bree Built A Tight End Store Nobody Shops At
teams.teaser: Four tight ends, one lineup slot, and a quarterback situation that begins and ends with Sam Darnold.
body: Puka Nacua, Chris Olave, CeeDee Lamb — a strong start, though Olave went with thirty better names still on the board, which means Bree took the receiver whose last three seasons ended early and skipped a room full of guys who finish games. Then the pivot. Tyler Warren, Colston Loveland, Sam LaPorta and Greg Dulcich. Four tight ends. One slot. Two of them rookies who've never caught a professional pass. Bree isn't drafting a position, she's opening a showroom.

The quarterback is Sam Darnold. Only Sam Darnold. In superflex, which starts two. She took him with fourteen better arms available, so this wasn't panic, it was preference — she looked at the board, saw quarterbacks, and reached past all of them for the one with the longest apology tour. Every Sunday one of her starting spots is going to be a tight end wearing a quarterback's number in her heart.

The backfield is a lottery drawer: Rico Dowdle, Kyle Monangai, Aaron Jones entering his age-31 season, Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Nobody there is a lock and everybody there is somebody's handcuff. Quentin Johnston in the twelfth completes the collection. Ka'imi Fairbairn kicks, 790 spots past necessity, and by then the tight end store had already closed for lack of foot traffic.

teams.verdict: Jay Collected Tight Ends Like Nobody Was Watching
teams.teaser: A gorgeous first six rounds, then four tight ends, one of whom retired and came back twice.
body: The top of this thing is disgusting in the good way. Jonathan Taylor, Kenneth Walker, Chase Brown, Drake London, Malik Nabers, DeVonta Smith. Six picks, six starters, zero mistakes. Jay had a plan. Jay executed the plan. Then round seven arrived and something happened to him that we may never fully understand.

Tucker Kraft with ten better players on the board. Then Evan Engram in the eleventh, thirty-two better names walked past. Then Darren Waller, who's entering his age-33 season after unretiring, which is a career arc, not a fantasy asset. That's four tight ends for one slot, and Jay somehow got there by reaching for three of them. He didn't fall into a tight end room. He built it, brick by brick, with intent.

The one quarterback is C.J. Stroud, taken in the eighth, in a format that starts two. So on Sunday, Jay's second quarterback is going to be Darren Waller, spiritually. Marvin Harrison Jr., Xavier Worthy and Calvin Ridley pad out the receivers, with Worthy and Ridley both taken well past sensible, which tells you the front of the draft used up all the discipline he had for the evening. Eddy Pineiro kicks. He may be the second-most reliable starter on the team.

teams.verdict: Tyler Drafted Receivers Until The Room Begged Him To Stop
teams.teaser: Eight wide receivers, three tight ends, and one running back who has to play every down of every game.
body: Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson back to back is a fine way to make enemies, and we'll grant that Tyler earned the first two rounds. Then it becomes a compulsion. DJ Moore, Zay Flowers, Jameson Williams, Wan'Dale Robinson, Rashid Shaheed. Eight receivers total. Moore came off the board with twenty-nine better players sitting there, which means Tyler wasn't drafting receivers because they were the best available. He was drafting receivers because that's the only aisle he walks down.

The running back is Chuba Hubbard. Singular. Round nine. In fifteen rounds Tyler drafted one man to carry the ball, and he's a guy whose job description changes every August. Meanwhile the tight ends piled up anyway — Jake Ferguson, Juwan Johnson, Terrance Ferguson — three of them, one slot, and a rookie in the mix for flavor. He hoarded the position he doesn't need while leaving the position he does need staffed by a volunteer.

At quarterback: Trevor Lawrence and Justin Herbert, and honestly, fine. That part works. But nobody drafted a kicker here, which means Tyler ran out of rounds before he ran out of receivers, and given the choice he'd take a ninth. Somewhere his lineup card has one RB slot, one TE slot, and a waiting room full of slot receivers who all think this is their year.

teams.verdict: Colin Opened A Tight End Retirement Home
teams.teaser: Five tight ends, two of them ancient, one lineup slot, and a backup quarterback who doesn't throw.
body: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Saquon Barkley, Javonte Williams — a genuinely strong opening, and then Colin found the tight end aisle and never left. Travis Kelce, entering his age-36 season. Mark Andrews, age 30 and coming off a year of everyone insisting he was finished. Isaiah Likely, AJ Barner. Four in seven rounds, five if you count the second Ravens tight end he took to make sure the first one had company. It's not depth. It's assisted living with a lineup slot.

The quarterback plan is Jordan Love and then, in the tenth round, Malik Willis. Willis has thrown fewer meaningful passes than most of Colin's tight ends have caught. In a format that starts two quarterbacks, the second one is a career backup taken with eight better arms still available, so Colin didn't settle for him. He chose him. Out loud.

Elsewhere: Tetairoa McMillan with nineteen better names on the board, Tony Pollard with twenty-five, Jerry Jeudy with twenty-six. A pattern emerges where Colin sees a full board and reaches anyway, like he's picking a restaurant on a road trip and refuses to check the exit sign. No kicker, because the rounds ran out. The orthopedic wing is fine. It's the geriatric wing that's at capacity.

teams.verdict: One Quarterback, Nine Receivers, Zero Regrets
teams.teaser: James drafted Joe Burrow, called the quarterback position solved, then spent eleven rounds hoarding receivers he'll never start.
body: Derrick Henry, entering his age-32 season, at 1.09, and honestly that's the fun kind of stubborn. Then Joe Burrow in the second and the quarterback room closed permanently. One quarterback. Superflex starts two. James looked at the single most important scarcity in this format and decided the solution was more wide receivers, which is like solving a flat tire by buying hubcaps.

And there are so many receivers. Garrett Wilson, Emeka Egbuka, Luther Burden, Michael Wilson, Matthew Golden, Jordan Addison. Six of them, three rookies, and Michael Wilson came off the board with twenty-six better players still available, which is a choice you can only make if you've stopped looking at the board and started looking inward. Burden went with twelve better names there. The theme isn't receivers. It's receivers nobody else wanted yet.

The backfield holds up — Omarion Hampton and TreVeyon Henderson are real, and MarShawn Lloyd in the eleventh with twenty-three better options is the tax James pays for enjoying himself. Trey McBride at tight end is the smartest pick on the roster and Oronde Gadsden in the thirteenth is the least. No kicker. Every Sunday James will start Joe Burrow and then stare at a bench of nine receivers, trying to decide which one can throw.

teams.verdict: Justin Drafted A Tight End Convention, Then Skipped Running Backs
teams.teaser: Four tight ends, seven receivers, and two running backs asked to shoulder an entire season between them.
body: Amon-Ra St. Brown and Lamar Jackson to open is the correct way to start a superflex draft, and Bo Nix in the third means Justin actually solved the position while half the room was pretending it didn't exist. Credit where it's due. Then the rest of the draft happened to him.

Harold Fannin Jr. in the fifth with thirteen better players there. Dallas Goedert in the eighth, age 31 and coming off a season where he was hurt more than he was healthy. Dalton Schultz in the twelfth. Four tight ends when the lineup asks for one, and one of them is a rookie he reached a full round for. Justin didn't need a tight end. He needed a hobby, and this became it.

The running backs are Quinshon Judkins, a rookie, and David Montgomery, entering his age-28 season with a lot of mileage — and Judkins went with eight better players on the board while Montgomery went with eight more. Two backs. Fifteen rounds. The receiver room, meanwhile, is a Jacksonville and Chicago swap meet: Rome Odunze, Christian Watson, Parker Washington, Brian Thomas Jr., Chris Godwin. Seven receivers, four tight ends, two running backs. Somewhere a lineup card has an RB2 slot and Justin's plan for it is a tight end and a prayer.

teams.verdict: Mike Built A Quarterback Room, And Not Much Else
teams.teaser: Five quarterbacks, zero running backs worth the name, and Jalen Hurts taken six picks before anybody was going to make him.
body: Mike took Jalen Hurts six picks before anyone was going to force his hand. Nobody was bidding. There was no rival in the room. He negotiated against himself and lost. Then Drake Maye, then Dak Prescott, then Jaxson Dart, then Daniel Jones. Five quarterbacks in six rounds, in a league that starts two, and the fifth one is Daniel Jones, taken with five better arms still available. Mike isn't drafting a roster. He's stockpiling a currency nobody in this league will trade for.

The running back situation is D'Andre Swift. That's it. One back, taken in the fifth, and then Mike never returned to the position for ten straight rounds. On Sunday he'll start Swift, then look at his bench, find four quarterbacks and a receiver, and put a quarterback in the flex because that's the whole plan and always was.

The receivers are actually decent — Tee Higgins, Terry McLaurin, Jakobi Meyers, Jayden Reed, KC Concepcion — which makes the rest of it stranger. Mike knew how to draft. He just kept choosing not to. Hunter Henry and Kenyon Sadiq handle tight end, and Sadiq's a rookie taken with four better names sitting there, because by round ten the habit was fully formed. No kicker. There wasn't room. The quarterbacks needed the space.

teams.verdict: Evan Drafted Two Backs, Then Retired From Roster Building
teams.teaser: A ruthless first four rounds followed by a scavenger hunt through the 2019 Pro Bowl roster.
body: James Cook, De'Von Achane, Patrick Mahomes, Brock Bowers. Four rounds, four studs, no notes. Evan had the best start in the room and clearly felt he'd done enough for one evening, because what follows is a tour through men whose best seasons are in the record books. Davante Adams, age 33. Aaron Rodgers, age 42, drafted in the eleventh round as the second quarterback in a format that starts two. Deebo Samuel, whose last productive year keeps getting further away. It's not a bench. It's a reunion.

The backfield stops at two. Cook, Achane, and then Rhamondre Stevenson in the eighth, and that's the entire ground game across fifteen rounds. Two of those three have to be healthy every single week for this to function, which is a lot to ask of two guys whose entire value is how often they touch the ball.

At tight end, Bowers, T.J. Hockenson and Pat Freiermuth — three for one slot, one of them the best in football and two of them expensive insurance he'll never cash. The receivers are Pickens, Waddle, Alec Pierce and Adams, which is fine, in the way a rental car is fine. No kicker. Evan's roster is a Ferrari with the back half of a golf cart welded on, and he'll still probably make the playoffs, which is the most annoying part.
